title: Gentle as a Mother, Encouraging as a Father
summary: Paul reminds the Thessalonians how he and his companions came to them after suffering in Philippi and preached the gospel boldly, not from deceit, greed, or desire for praise. They were gentle like a nursing mother, worked night and day so as not to be a burden, and urged each believer like a father to live worthily of God. Paul thanks God that the church received his message as God's word, even though it brought persecution, and he tells them how much he longs to see them.
story: Chapter 1 described the church's conversion; chapter 2 turns to the messengers. Paul had been forced out of Thessalonica after only a short stay, leaving a young church behind under persecution. In a city full of traveling speakers who took money and moved on, his sudden departure could look like one more charlatan's exit. So Paul reminds the believers of what they saw with their own eyes: the conduct of people who shared not only the gospel but their own lives. The chapter ends by turning from the past to the present, explaining that Paul's absence is not indifference, which leads into Timothy's mission in chapter 3.
historical:
Verse 2 refers to the events of Acts 16:19-40, where Paul and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into prison in Philippi before being released and asked to leave the city. They came on to Thessalonica, about 100 miles (160 km) southwest along the Via Egnatia, and preached despite the danger. Opposition arose there too: Acts 17:5-9 describes a mob that attacked the house of Jason, where they were staying, and dragged Jason before the city officials, forcing Paul and Silas to leave by night.

Verses 14 to 16 connect the Thessalonians' sufferings at the hands of their own countrymen with the sufferings of the churches in Judea at the hands of some of their Jewish neighbors. Paul himself had once been among those persecuting the church in Judea (Galatians 1:13, 22-23). Verse 16 says wrath has come upon them, and scholars debate what Paul had in view: perhaps a recent disaster such as the expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2, around AD 49), or unrest in Judea, or a statement about the certainty of coming judgment spoken as though already present.
cultural:
The Greek world was full of wandering teachers and philosophers, some serious and many not, who went from city to city giving speeches and seeking followers, fees, or patrons. Critics accused many of flattery, greed, and self-promotion. Abraham Malherbe showed that Paul's language here closely parallels descriptions of the ideal philosopher in the writings of Dio Chrysostom, a Greek orator of the late first century, who contrasted the true philosopher's boldness and gentleness with the frauds. Paul claims the marks of the true teacher: boldness under opposition, freedom from deceit and flattery, no greed, no seeking of glory, and gentleness.

Paul worked at a trade (Acts 18:3 says he was a tentmaker or leatherworker) so that he would not depend on his hearers for support. Manual labor was looked down on by the elite, and a teacher who worked with his hands would have been noticed. The images of the nursing mother and the father drew on familiar roles: a nurse (often a hired wet nurse, but here caring for her own children) was a picture of tender devotion, and a father was responsible for the moral education of his children.
literary: The chapter is a personal defense and remembrance, though whether Paul was answering specific accusations or simply drawing a contrast with common frauds is debated. It is built on appeals to memory (you know, you recall, you are witnesses) and on sharp contrasts: not deceit but approval by God, not pleasing people but God, not flattery or greed but gentleness, not a burden but hard work. Two family images frame the central section: a nursing mother (verse 7) and a father (verse 11). A second thanksgiving (verse 13) contrasts the word of men with the word of God. Verses 14 to 16 contain a harsh statement about Judean opponents, and verses 17 to 20 shift to Paul's longing, using the image of a child orphaned from parents (the verb in verse 17) and closing with the church as his crown at the Lord's coming.

outline.t: Not flattery, greed, or seeking glory
Like a nursing mother and a father
Receiving God's word and suffering for it
Torn away and longing to return

doctrines.note: The Thessalonians received Paul's message not as the word of men but as what it truly is, the word of God, which is at work in those who believe (verse 13). God speaks through human messengers, and his word is active, not merely informative.

Paul's picture of ministry is shared life: he and his companions gave the church not only the gospel but their own lives (verse 8). Leadership in the church is modeled on parents' care, gentle and demanding, not on the self-promotion of public speakers.

The Thessalonians suffered at the hands of their own countrymen, as the Judean churches did, and as Jesus and the prophets did before them (verses 14 and 15). Persecution for the gospel places believers in a long line of faithful sufferers.

words.note: Nepios, infant or little child. Verse 7 has a famous textual question. Many early manuscripts read nepioi, we were infants among you, while others read epioi, we were gentle, a difference of one letter in Greek. The underlying text used here has infants, though the Berean Standard Bible translates gentle. Scholars are divided: the manuscript evidence favors infants, but gentle fits the following image of a nursing mother more smoothly. Either way, Paul stresses that he did not throw his weight around.

Trophos, nurse. The word could refer to a wet nurse or to a mother nursing her own children, as the phrase her own children suggests here. It is an image of tender, costly care. Paul, who could have insisted on his authority as an apostle, chooses a picture of a mother feeding and warming her infant.

Parousia, coming or presence. The word was used for the arrival of a ruler or official on a state visit, often with great ceremony. This is the first time the letter uses it for the return of Jesus (verse 19). Paul imagines standing before the Lord at his coming and presenting the Thessalonians as his joy and crown.

christ: Paul's conduct among the Thessalonians reflects the pattern of Christ, who came not to be served but to serve. His gentleness, his refusal to be a burden, and his willingness to share his life echo the Lord he preached. Jesus is also named as one who suffered: he was killed, like the prophets before him (verse 15), and his followers share his rejection. The gospel is the gospel of God (verses 2, 8, and 9), but its center is Christ, who calls believers into God's own kingdom and glory (verse 12). The chapter ends looking toward the coming of the Lord Jesus, when Paul expects to stand before him with the Thessalonians as his glory and joy.

hard.a: These verses say that some Jews killed the Lord Jesus and the prophets, drove Paul out, displease God, oppose all people, and face wrath. After centuries of Christian hostility toward Jews, the passage has been read with great pain, and it has been misused. Several points help. Paul was himself a Jew, as were Jesus, the apostles, and the churches in Judea he describes as suffering. He is speaking of particular opponents in Judea who persecuted the church and hindered his mission to the Gentiles, in the same way that the Thessalonians suffered from their own Gentile countrymen; the comparison is between persecutors, not between races. His language resembles the prophets' own denunciations of Israel's leaders, a form of criticism from inside. Elsewhere Paul expresses great sorrow for his fellow Jews and hope for their salvation (Romans 9 to 11). A minority of scholars have argued that verses 15 and 16 were added by a later hand after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, but no manuscript lacks them, and most scholars accept them as Paul's. The passage can never be used to justify contempt for the Jewish people.

questions: Paul says he shared not only the gospel but his own life. What is the difference between those two, and why does it matter?
What would it look like for a leader today to be gentle like a nursing mother and encouraging like a father?
How can you tell the difference between someone who speaks to please God and someone who speaks to please people?
